title: Paper Explained: ActCam: Zero-Shot Joint Camera and 3D Motion Control for Video Generation - A Beginner's Guide
subtitle: Create videos with actors moving and cameras adjusting without training

content.background:
Before this work, people who wanted to generate videos with moving characters and changing camera angles faced a big catch: you could either control the character’s motion or the camera, but not both in a way that stays consistent across the whole video. Many existing tools needed extra training on every new scene, which is slow and costly. If you tried to move the camera around a performer, the result often looked off—the person could wobble, props or the background wouldn’t line up in 3D, or the motion would lose its natural feel. In short, there was a gap between making a believable performance and making a believable camera shot, and nothing easy or quick enough to combine both in one go.

This limitation mattered a lot for artists and filmmakers who want to reuse a great performance in many different scenes and shot setups. Being able to transfer how someone moves from one video into a new setting, while also freely choosing how the camera moves frame by frame, would unlock a lot of creative experimentation without reshooting or collecting endless new data. A system that works in a “zero-shot” way—without training a new model for each job—would also lower the barrier for students and hobbyists to play with cinematic videos. The motivation behind this research is to give creators a robust, flexible tool that jointly respects both motion and viewpoint, so they can craft convincing, movie-like sequences more easily and with less prior work.
content.methodology:
ActCam is a zero-shot method that lets you control both how a character moves and how the camera frames that motion in a generated video, without needing to train a new model. The idea is to take advantage of a pretrained image-to-video diffusion model that can be guided by two kinds of information: where the character is and how the scene is structured in depth. You provide (1) a driving video showing the character’s motion and (2) a plan for how the camera should move. ActCam then produces a video where the actor follows the driving motion and the camera follows the target path, while keeping the scene geometry consistent from frame to frame.

How it works, conceptually, in a few steps:
- Step 1: extract the motion. From the driving video, the system derives per-frame character poses (how the joints and limbs are arranged) so it knows what motion to transfer.
- Step 2: prepare depth and pose guidance. For each frame, it also generates or estimates depth cues that help the model understand the scene’s 3D layout. The target camera motion is converted into a sequence of conditioning prompts that the diffusion model can use.
- Step 3: two-phase conditioning during a single sample. The generation runs in one pass with a clever schedule:
  - Early denoising steps condition on both pose and sparse depth. This helps lock in the overall structure and ensures the actor’s motion and the scene’s geometry stay aligned.
  - Later steps drop the depth guidance and rely on pose-only guidance to refine high-frequency details (like clothing folds or facial features) without over-constraining the scene.
- Step 4: produce the video. The result is a sequence where the actor moves as in the driving video, the camera follows the planned trajectory, and the viewpoint changes remain geometrically coherent across frames.

Why this matters and what it achieves:
- It’s zero-shot, meaning you don’t train on new scenes to get joint camera and motion control; it leverages a strong, pre-trained diffusion model with depth and pose conditioning.
- Compared with methods that only control pose or that jointly control pose and camera but require extra training, ActCam tends to better match the camera path and the character’s motion, especially when the viewpoint changes a lot. Human evaluators tend to prefer ActCam in challenging scenarios.
- The key ideas are careful camera-consistent conditioning (keeping depth and pose aligned over time) and the staged guidance (first set the structure with depth, then refine details with pose). Together, they enable strong two-way control—you can steer both how the actor moves and how the camera moves—without retraining the model.

If you want a quick mental picture: imagine directing a film where you have a motion-captured dancer and a moving camera. ActCam acts like a smart director’s assistant that translates the dancer’s motion into a new scene, plans where the camera should go, and then guides the filming process in two stages so the audience sees a believable 3D space and fluid movement. Project page: https://elkhomar.github.io/actcam/.
content.results:
ActCam is a zero-shot method for making a moving character appear in a new scene while also controlling how the camera moves from frame to frame. In simple terms, you take a video of an actor moving, tell ActCam how you want the camera to travel, and it generates a new video where the actor’s motion fits the new scene and the camera path you specified. It does this without retraining a model on the new scene. It relies on a prebuilt image-to-video diffusion model that can take two kinds of hints each frame: where things are in 3D (depth) and how the character is posed. ActCam combines these hints so the scene stays coherent across frames as the camera moves.

A key idea behind ActCam is a two-step conditioning process during generation. In the first phase, the model uses both pose and sparse depth information to establish the overall layout and geometry of the scene, helping the video stay consistent as objects move and the camera changes viewpoint. In the second phase, the depth guidance is reduced and the model focuses on refining the character’s details driven by pose alone. This staged approach lets the system keep solid scene structure early on, then add fine, high-frequency details without over-constraining the motion or the visuals.

Compared to previous methods, ActCam stands out because it achieves joint control over both the actor’s motion and the camera path without any additional training (zero-shot). Earlier approaches often handled pose or camera control in isolation or required training on new scenes, which limited flexibility and made large camera viewpoint changes tricky to pull off. ActCam delivers better alignment with the requested camera motion and more faithful motion of the character, and human evaluators preferred its results, especially when the camera swung a lot or changed angles. Practically, this means artists and filmmakers can quickly prototype or create videos where a performer moves in a new environment with a specified camera journey, all without collecting new training data or building specialized models.
content.significance:
ActCam matters today because it shows how you can steer both how a character moves and how the camera views the scene—without having to train a new model for each project. It uses a driving video to transfer motion to a new scene and lets you control per-frame camera parameters (like where the camera is and how it’s tilted) while keeping the action geometrically consistent across frames. The key trick is a two-phase conditioning strategy: first, you guide the early denoising steps with both pose and a sparse depth map to establish the scene’s structure; then you drop the depth and let pose guidance refine the details. This makes the generated video look coherent from different viewpoints and still feel like a real performance, which is hard to achieve with naïve, frame-by-frame generation.

In the longer term, ActCam helped push the field toward true joint control of 3D structure and motion in video generation. Its ideas—conditioning diffusion models with geometric cues (pose and depth), doing zero-shot transfer from existing footage, and using staged guidance to balance structure with detail—became a blueprint for later work on 3D-aware, controllable video. The approach lowered the barrier to high-quality, cinematic video creation: non-experts can craft complex scenes by specifying motion and camera intent rather than needing large, labeled training datasets or custom models. This laid groundwork for more integrated virtual production tools where actors, cameras, and scenes can be manipulated in a user-friendly, physically plausible way.

There are clear applications and influences in today’s AI tooling. In film, game development, and social media content creation, creators now expect systems that can retarget character motion to new scenes and keep camera motion believable across angles. Modern diffusion-based video tools and virtual production workflows—such as those seen in platforms like Runway Gen-2 and Meta/NVIDIA-inspired pipelines—embody the same spirit of controllability through pose, depth, and camera parameters. On a broader note, ActCam connects to how large AI systems like ChatGPT operate: you plan with structured constraints (motion plus camera) and then execute in phases to refine details. It’s a practical example of how multi-modal, controllable generative AI can decompose a complex task into a planning stage and a refinement stage, a pattern that shows up across contemporary AI products and will shape future, more capable video and virtual-reality tools.

concept_explanation.title: Understanding Two-Phase Conditioning: The Heart of ActCam
concept_explanation.content:
Imagine you’re directing a tiny movie with a puppet and a movable camera. You want the puppet to move exactly like in a driving video, but you also want the camera to sweep around it in a new, cinematic way. Do this well and the result feels like a real scene: the actor’s motion stays faithful, and the camera path looks natural. ActCam does this with a clever two-phase conditioning idea. It guides a video generator first with rough structural cues (where things are in space and how the camera moves), then later relaxes those constraints a bit to polish details without breaking the overall structure.

Here’s how it works step by step. First, you start with a pretrained image-to-video diffusion model that can take conditioning inputs such as the character’s pose and depth information about the scene. From the source driving video, you extract the moving character’s pose for each frame. You also create a sparse depth hint for each frame—think of it as a rough map of depth that tells you where the floor, characters, and major surfaces are, but not a complete 3D model. The target is a new camera motion, so you also specify how the camera should move over time. With these ingredients, you run the diffusion model in a single sampling pass, but in two phases. Phase one uses both the pose data and the sparse depth to steer the generation toward a coherent scene layout and correct-camera alignment. Phase two drops the depth conditioning but keeps the pose guidance, letting the model refine textures, shading, and fine details without over-constraining the geometry.

A concrete example helps. Suppose the driving video shows a dancer weaving across a studio, and you want the dancer to perform the same motions but in a different outdoor scene with a camera circling around. In Phase 1, the model uses the dancer’s per-frame poses plus the sparse depth cues (rough floor level, nearby objects, and general scene depth) to place the dancer correctly in space and to keep the camera on a smooth, planned path. This helps the model avoid collapsing into awkward positions or drifting the dancer out of frame as the viewpoint changes. In Phase 2, depth guidance is removed, and the model focuses on making the dancer’s clothes, hair, and lighting look natural, while the motion stays faithful to the original choreography. The result is a video where the camera movement remains true to the target path and the motion looks sharp and believable, even with big changes in viewpoint.

Why is this two-phase approach important? It lets you achieve strong joint control over both camera motion and character motion without needing to train a new model for every combination. The early phase fixes the big picture—where things sit in the scene and how the camera travels—so the final frames don’t wander off into implausible geometry. The later phase then adds the fine details that make the video feel real, without re-imposing the broad structure in a way that would smother motion or create stiff visuals. This balance is especially valuable when you want large viewpoint changes or to reuse a single model across many actors and scenes, which is exactly what makes ActCam appealing for zero-shot video generation.

In terms of practical use, think of it as a tool for film and game production, virtual production, or any project where you want to transfer a performer’s motion into a new location with precise camera control. You could use it to generate rehearsal footage from a standard acting take, create cinematic drone-like camera moves around a dancing character, or prototype camera designs for a scene before shooting. A key practical note is that you need a capable depth cue (even if sparse) and reliable pose extraction from the driving video. The two-phase conditioning is where the magic happens: it keeps the scene coherent at the macro level while still letting the image-level details shine, enabling high-quality, camera-consistent motion transfer without extra training.

summary: ActCam is a zero-shot method that jointly controls a character’s motion and the camera in generated videos by transferring motion from a driving video to a new scene and conditioning a pretrained diffusion model on pose and depth with a two-phase guidance that first enforces structure and then refines details, achieving better camera adherence and motion fidelity without any training.
